2	
3	No spike was run: every open question needing a browser or iPhone is not runnable here, and none of the rest needs an experiment. `git status` is clean.
4	
5	## Settled
6	
7	### The tree
8	
9	- A leaked pairing code is short-lived: the window closes on the first successful pairing, after 3 wrong codes, or at 5 minutes. `src/core/remote.rs:46-72` (`Paired` clears `pairing`, "single-use").
10	- `RemoteRequest` is built only inside `src/adapters/remote.rs` (definition `:360`); no test in `tests/` constructs it. Adding `cookie`, `origin` and `user_agent` fields touches the adapter alone. Grep: `RemoteRequest\b` over `src tests`.
11	- `RemoteReply { status, body, authenticated }` is built literally at about 15 sites in `src/app.rs` (e.g. `:1664`, `:2365`, `:2754`, `:3570`, `:3723`, `:3736`, `:3767`) and not in `tests/`. A header field on it needs a `Default` or a constructor, or every site changes.
12	- `RemoteRequest` and `RemoteReply` live in `adapters/`, not `ports/` or `model.rs`, so CLAUDE.md's additivity rule for the shared contract does not name them. `src/adapters/remote.rs:355-393`.
13	- `last_message` exists on the session record: the hook binary writes it from `last_assistant_message` (`src/bin/switchboard-hook.rs:37`) and `src/core/tests.rs:1717` constructs records with `last_message: None`. It is not on the wire: no match in `control/` or `client/Sources`. Adding it to `SessionView` is a new field there.
14	- The certificate can be reissued over the same key. `rcgen::KeyPair::from_pem` is already used at `src/adapters/remote.rs:139,146`, the SPKI hash is of the key (`:107`), and `make_identity` (`:95-127`) is the only path that makes a new key. A reissue keeps `spki_sha256`.
15	- `PairingInvite` is used by `ConnectionManager.swift`, `BrowserView.swift`, `switchboard-remote/main.swift` and eight test files under `client/Tests`. `addresses` is read as a list at `ConnectionManager.swift:483` and built as a one-element list at `main.swift:120`. A URL parser can fill `addresses` with the one host:port.
16	
17	### Outside the tree
18	
19	- **Apple's TLS server certificate rules.** SHA-2 signature, RSA at least 2048 bits, the server's DNS name in subjectAltName (CommonName not trusted), and for certificates issued after 1 July 2019 an EKU of `serverAuth` and a validity of at most 825 days. Non-compliant connections fail and "websites [may] not load in Safari". Evidence: https://support.apple.com/103769 (iOS 13 / macOS 10.15; Citrix says iOS 14 / macOS 11 also). The page does not mention IP-address SANs, user-added roots, or exemptions. The current certificate has no SAN, a CN only, and a not-after of year 4096 (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95-127`), so it meets none of the SAN, EKU or validity rules.
20	- **Safari and `wss://` after a click-through.** The behaviour exists and is unfixed: WebKit bug 41419 ("allow wss:// if user has accepted https:// warning") is open, status NEW, last modified 2026-01-12, and the reporter got `wss` working only after marking the certificate always-trusted (https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=41419). code-server's iPad doc agrees: Safari "will prevent WebSocket connections unless the certificate is installed as a profile", needs a domain name rather than a bare IP, and needs a SAN matching the host (https://github.com/cdr/code-server/blob/v3.7.0/doc/ipad.md). Two sources agree; they cover Safari up to 2026-01. One more report is mixed: on iOS 26 beta 3, `wss` failed after acceptance and the poster said it was resolved in beta 5 (https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/792842). That is a forum post, a lead only.
21	  - Queries: "Safari iOS WebSocket wss self-signed certificate accepted exception fails fetch works"; "iOS Safari self-signed certificate no subjectAltName IP address proceed certificate warning".
22	- **Secure contexts.** `crypto.randomUUID()` is available only in secure contexts (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Crypto/randomUUID). The spec decides trustworthiness by the origin's scheme: `https` and `wss` are "Potentially Trustworthy", with no mention of certificate errors (https://w3c.github.io/webappsec-secure-contexts/ §3.1; MDN Secure_Contexts agrees). By the text, an https page on a click-through certificate is a secure context. Whether browsers also treat it so is not stated, and it is under Unresolved.
23	- **Cookies are not isolated by port.** RFC 6265 says so, quoted on https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Cookies. `Secure` cookies are sent only over HTTPS. `localStorage` is per origin including port (MDN, general). This confirms the notes' cross-port claim.
24	- **WebSocket subprotocol (RFC 6455 §4.1, §4.2.2, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455).**
25	  - The client must fail if the 101 names a subprotocol it did not offer.
26	  - The server's reply is one `token`, and an empty value is illegal.
27	  - Offered values are `token`s, so base64url without padding is legal. Base64 `=` is not a token character (a separator).
28	  - Whether the client must fail when the server returns none is not normative: §4.2.2 says the server sends none when it agrees to none, and §1.9 (non-normative) says it must include it.
29	  - Browsers must send `Origin` on the handshake. A server may validate it, and rejects with 403. "If the server does not validate the origin, it will accept connections from anywhere."
30	  - The tree's `respond_upgrade` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:519-527`) echoes no subprotocol.
31	- **`history.replaceState` replaces the current entry**; Back then shows the new URL and bypasses the old one (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/History/replaceState). It says nothing about what the browser recorded before the script ran.
32	  - Query: "MDN history.replaceState".
33	
34	## Unresolved
35	
36	Each line ends with what the plan builds to. The plan never waits on a line here.
37	
38	1. **Does a click-through exception cover `wss://` and `fetch` on current iOS Safari, with this no-SAN certificate on a bare IP?**
39	   - Tried: the queries above, plus "Safari remember certificate exception visit this website how long self-signed iOS per session". The only evidence is old (2010 bug, iOS 7 and 13 era), the code-server doc (v3.7, 2021), and the one iOS 26 beta post. Nothing current and primary exists.
40	   - Favourable: the page may use the events socket directly. Unfavourable, and the plan must do this anyway: the page works with REST polling alone (poll `changed`-equivalent reads on a timer) and treats the socket as an upgrade it may lose, saying "live updates unavailable" rather than failing.
41	   - Reissuing the certificate with a SAN, `serverAuth` and a bounded validity over the same key is cheap and helps in both cases (Apple's page; the code-server doc).
42	2. **Does a SAN with an IP address, rather than a DNS name, satisfy Safari and Chrome?** The Apple page speaks only of DNS names. Queries: as in 1, plus "iOS Safari self-signed certificate no subjectAltName IP address". No primary source found.
43	   - Favourable: put the LAN IP in the SAN. Unfavourable: the page's URL host must be a `.local` name. Either way the plan reissues with the `.local` hostname as a DNS SAN as well.
44	3. **Does Apple's 825-day rule apply to a manually trusted self-signed leaf?** The page lists no exemption and no scope. Build to a validity of 825 days or fewer and say in the dialog that the certificate is renewed (the key, and so the pin, is unchanged). If it does not apply, nothing is lost.
45	4. **Does a click-through certificate give a secure context in Safari, Chrome and Firefox?** The spec reads yes by scheme, but I found no browser documentation on certificate-error overrides. The plan uses `crypto.randomUUID` only when `window.isSecureContext`, with a fallback id generator built on `getRandomValues`, and does not rely on `Secure` cookies being stored without a manual test (see item 5).
46	5. **Are `SameSite=Strict` cookies sent on a same-origin `new WebSocket()` handshake, and do `Secure` cookies work on an IP host, in Safari, Chrome and Firefox?** Query: "SameSite=Strict cookie sent on same-origin WebSocket handshake; Secure cookie IP address host Safari Chrome Firefox". Results were blogs and a Chromium design thread (WebSocket requests carry cookies; `wss` counts as the same scheme as `https`): leads, not evidence. Plan to either transport behind one server-side reader that accepts the bearer header, the cookie and the subprotocol token, and let the first manual run pick the page's transport.
47	6. **Is the code-bearing URL recorded in history, tab list or iCloud tab sync before `replaceState` runs?** No source. The plan assumes yes: the code is single-use and the window is 5 minutes or 3 failures (settled above), so a recorded URL is dead once pairing succeeds. The plan says that in the dialog and keeps the query out of server logs (`refuse`, `src/app.rs:3754`, logs path only).
48	7. **Per-site exception lifetime across launches, and loss when the IP changes.** Query: "Safari remember certificate exception ... how long". Only a 2013 blog (iOS 7: exception not removable). Plan: an address change means another warning, and the page and dialog say so. A `.local` name or a reissue never makes it worse.
49	8. **Pool of 4 under a real page load (iOS Safari parallel connections, keep-alive, `/favicon.ico`).** No source for the connection count; it needs a device. Plan: answer static paths on the connection thread with `Connection: close`, serve the page as few files as possible (HTML plus one script and one stylesheet, inlined where possible by the CSP), and give static paths their own bound so a page load cannot starve `/pair`.
50	9. **Bonjour `.local` resolution from iOS Safari.** No query run, so no evidence. Plan: the URL carries the IP from `local_address()` and the `.local` name only if the owner answers item B below.
51	
52	## For the owner
53	
54	A. **On a real iPhone/iPad, after accepting the warning, does the page load, do `fetch` calls work, and does `new WebSocket("wss://…")` connect, with the current certificate and with the reissued one?** Ask with the page as built. Favourable branch: use the socket. Unfavourable: ship polling. The plan builds the polling path regardless.
55	B. **Does `https://<mac-name>.local:<port>/` resolve from the owner's phone?** Favourable: reissue with that DNS SAN and put it in the URL. Unfavourable: the IP stays the URL host. Reissuing with both works either way.
56	C. **Does the owner's phone camera open the URL straight into Safari, and does the tab appear in iCloud tab sync or history before the page script runs?** Either branch: the code is single-use and expires, so the plan holds.
57	D. **Does a cookie, or a subprotocol token, work in Safari with the owner's certificate (items 5, 1)?** Favourable: use the one that works, the cookie preferred for the token never being readable by script. Unfavourable: use the other; the server accepts all three transports regardless.

1	# Issue #230: a browser page on the remote port, investigation notes
2	
3	Read: CLAUDE.md, docs/lessons.md (84 lines, nothing about the remote port;
4	its lesson is the action/effect core, a fake for every port, and "spike
5	risky technology first"), docs/remote-client.md §§0–5, design.md "Trust
6	boundary" (l.219) and the start of "Remote client (2026-10-12)" (l.3107),
7	plus the code below. Line numbers are as they are in this worktree at
8	7fe8949. There is no `web/` directory yet.
9	
10	## The record first: what is on disk, and how it comes back
11	
12	- **No new record kind and no `model.rs` change is needed.** A browser is
13	  one more `PairedDevice` (`src/ports/remote.rs:96-107`: `id`, `name`,
14	  `scope`, `token_sha256`, `created`, `last_seen`) in
15	  `<data dir>/devices.json`. That file is a bare `Vec<PairedDevice>`
16	  with no schema version (`RemoteFiles::load_devices`/`save_devices`,
17	  `src/adapters/remote.rs:80-86`), written atomically by
18	  `Effect::SaveDevices` (`src/core/remote.rs:121-125`). The name comes
19	  from `/pair`'s `device_name` (`src/app.rs:3650-3655`), cut to 64 chars
20	  in `AppCore::new_device` (`src/core/remote.rs:166-175`). So "Safari on
21	  iPhone" can be the page's own `device_name` with no host change. If
22	  the plan wants a `kind` (browser or native) on the device, it is an
23	  additive `#[serde(default)]` field in a file that has no version.
24	- **Rehydration** is unchanged: `IdentityLoaded { identity, devices,
25	  rotated }` (`src/core/remote.rs:22-30`) puts the devices back at
26	  launch. A token is checked by hash against them on every request
27	  (`authenticate`, `src/app.rs:3125-3153`; `device_by_token`,
28	  `src/core/remote.rs:145-147`). Revoke (`RevokeDevice`,
29	  `src/core/remote.rs:86-92`) and scope change (`:93-100`) apply on the
30	  next request, and revoke closes the device's socket (test
31	  `revoke_closes_the_devices_socket`, `tests/remote.rs:2892`).
32	- **The pairing window is not durable** (`PairingWindow` in core state:
33	  code, scope, `until`, failures; `OpenPairing`/`ClosePairing`/
34	  `PairingFailed`/`Paired`, `src/core/remote.rs:46-73`). The QR is built
35	  in the UI from it (`src/ui/remote.rs:155-173`). Changing JSON to a URL
36	  is a change to that `json!` call and to the "Copy invite" text (`:199-206`),
37	  not to any record.
38	- **The page itself is not a record.** It is static bytes compiled in
39	  (`include_str!`). On the device, what persists is the token, plus
40	  whatever the page keeps to say "identity changed". Decision 2 picks
41	  where that is. The browser also keeps its certificate exception per
42	  host. The host keeps nothing new per browser beyond the device record.
43	- **Identity** (`identity.json`, `Identity` at `src/ports/remote.rs:26-42`,
44	  `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION = 1` at `:17`). It holds the certificate
45	  (base64 DER) and `spki_sha256`. The certificate is made by
46	  `make_identity` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95-127`) with
47	  `CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())`: **no subjectAltName at
48	  all**, a CN of `Switchboard <server_id>`, rcgen's default validity
49	  (the comment says `not_after` is the year 4096), and no EKU set
50	  explicitly. The native clients pin the SPKI and ignore names, so this
51	  never mattered. A browser checks names and validity. Changing the
52	  certificate (adding SANs for the LAN address or a `.local` name, or a
53	  bounded validity) changes nothing the pin sees if the key is reused
54	  (the SPKI is the same, §5). But the certificate is stored in
55	  `identity.json`, so reissuing it means writing that file, and an
56	  address that moves would need another reissue.
57	
58	## What the code does today, piece by piece
59	
60	### The listener (`src/adapters/remote.rs`)
61	
62	- `read_request` (`:444-513`) keeps the method, the path, the query
63	  (undecoded), the body, `bearer` (`Authorization: Bearer`, `:487-491`)
64	  and `upgrade` (`Sec-WebSocket-Key` when `Upgrade: websocket`,
65	  `:492-495`). It throws away every other header. **It does not read
66	  `Cookie`, `Origin`, `User-Agent`, `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, `Host`,
67	  `If-None-Match` or `Accept`.** Either token transport in decision 2
68	  needs a new `RemoteRequest` field. That struct is in
69	  `src/adapters/remote.rs:359-372`, which is not under `ports/`, but
70	  `tests/remote.rs` builds requests and should be checked.
71	- `respond` (`:530-552`) always writes `Content-Type: application/json`
72	  and `Connection: keep-alive`, nothing else. It has no CSP, no
73	  Cache-Control, no Set-Cookie and no other content type. `RemoteReply`
74	  (`:388-393`) is `{status, body, authenticated}`. Static files and a
75	  cookie on `/pair` therefore need `RemoteReply` (or a separate
76	  connection-thread path) to carry headers. `respond_upgrade`
77	  (`:519-527`) writes no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`. A browser that offered
78	  a subprotocol fails the handshake if the server does not echo one
79	  (that is a question below, not checked).
80	- Pools and windows: `MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED = 4`, `MAX_PAIRED = 12`
81	  (`:567-568`). A stream past the 4 is dropped at accept (`:699-706`). A
82	  connection moves pools only when a reply says `authenticated: true`
83	  (`:834-849`). `HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT` is 5 s (`:570`), and the first
84	  request line has the same deadline. `IDLE_TIMEOUT` is 30 s (`:573`).
85	  The rate windows exist only for `/api/v1/pair` (6/min) and
86	  `/api/v1/info` (60/min) (`:583-587`, `Limits::limited` `:629-640`).
87	  Any other path, a static one included, is unlimited and goes to the
88	  frame. What this means for a page load: a browser opens several
89	  parallel connections and keeps them alive. Static GETs leave a

  one more `PairedDevice` (`src/ports/remote.rs:96-107`: `id`, `name`,
  `scope`, `token_sha256`, `created`, `last_seen`) in
  `<data dir>/devices.json`. That file is a bare `Vec<PairedDevice>`
  with no schema version (`RemoteFiles::load_devices`/`save_devices`,
  `src/adapters/remote.rs:80-86`), written atomically by
  `Effect::SaveDevices` (`src/core/remote.rs:121-125`). The name comes
  from `/pair`'s `device_name` (`src/app.rs:3650-3655`), cut to 64 chars
  in `AppCore::new_device` (`src/core/remote.rs:166-175`). So "Safari on
  iPhone" can be the page's own `device_name` with no host change. If
  the plan wants a `kind` (browser or native) on the device, it is an
  additive `#[serde(default)]` field in a file that has no version.

  rotated }` (`src/core/remote.rs:22-30`) puts the devices back at
  launch. A token is checked by hash against them on every request

  `src/core/remote.rs:145-147`). Revoke (`RevokeDevice`,
  `src/core/remote.rs:86-92`) and scope change (`:93-100`) apply on the
  next request, and revoke closes the device's socket (test
  `revoke_closes_the_devices_socket`, `tests/remote.rs:2892`).

  where that is. The browser also keeps its certificate exception per

  never mattered. A browser checks names and validity. Changing the

  bounded validity) changes nothing the pin sees if the key is reused

  otherwise. Both are content keys that need `watch` frames on the
  socket for `changed` (§4.4 "Watch frames"). The page must speak
  `watch`/`unwatch`, wait for `watching`, then fetch.
- Reply box: `POST sessions/{id}/send` with `{op, text}` under `control`
  (`remote_command`, `:3159`). The page makes the op (needs
  `crypto.randomUUID`, which only exists in a secure context; see
  questions) and follows §4.5's `/ops/{op}` rule on a timeout.

### Pairing UI and the text paths

- QR payload: `src/ui/remote.rs:160-166`, a JSON object with
  `addresses` holding at most one `ip:port` from `remote::local_address()`
  (`src/adapters/remote.rs:962-970`, the outward route's source
  address). An IPv6 result would need brackets in a URL. The address is
  whatever the route picks, not necessarily the one the phone reaches.
- Swift: `PairingInvite.parse` decodes JSON only
  (`client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:93-116`).
  `switchboard-remote pair '<invite json>'` or `pair <host:port> <code>
  <spki>` (`client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift:12-13,
  107-125`). `PairingInvite` is used by `ConnectionManager.swift`,
  `BrowserView.swift` and eight test files under `client/Tests`. Taking a
  URL means `parse` tries URL first (`URLComponents`, `code`/`key`/`id`)
  and JSON second. `addresses` comes from the URL's host and port.
- The README dev-aid text (l.265-278) documents "Copy invite" as the QR
  text and `switchboard-remote pair "$(pbpaste)"`. It must change with
  the payload.
- The script line `pairing <code>` (README l.278, `src/script.rs`) opens
  a window with a known code. That is enough to drive the page by hand
  against a test data dir.

### Tests that exist and what extends

- `tests/remote.rs` speaks raw HTTP/1.1 over a pinned rustls client
  (`http`, `:245-296`). It reads `Content-Length` only and keeps no other
  header, so header assertions (CSP, Cache-Control, Set-Cookie,
  Content-Type) need it to return headers. The relevant neighbours are
  `info_is_served_to_anyone_and_every_other_read_is_refused_unpaired`
  (`:426`), `the_allowlist_refuses_everything_else_with_no_side_effect`
  (`:682`), `pair_is_rate_limited_per_listener` (`:1406`),
  `subscribe_at` (`:1960`) and `the_client_fixtures_decode_on_both_sides`
  (`:1829`, `client/Fixtures`).
- "Every path the page references is served" can be a test over the
  embedded strings. The page is plain JS with no runner in the tree, so
  its logic (query parse, `replaceState`, revision reconcile) is
  untested unless the plan adds a JS test harness, which the issue rules
  out as a dependency. The page's protocol logic is therefore checked
  only by hand.
- CI runs on Linux. `include_str!` of `web/*` is portable.

## Things the issue asserts that the tree contradicts or leaves open

- "Any path outside `/api/v1/` is refused": true (`src/app.rs:3023`), but
  on the frame, after the request was queued (so it costs inbox space),
  not at the connection thread.
- "the one-line excerpt the card shows" is not on the wire (above).
- "the device's scope in the header": no endpoint returns it after
  pairing (above).
- "'revoked' said plainly": the refusal code does not distinguish it
  (above).
- The `key` check in the page compares the URL's key with what `/info`
  says. A page cannot read the TLS certificate it is talking over, so
  this proves only that the host *claims* that key. A relay forwards
  `/info` faithfully, and the host's own `spki_sha256` check in
  `remote_pair` (`:3639-3647`) is fed by the page's body, which is the
  impostor's page under a relay. What it does catch is a genuine page on
  the wrong genuine host (a second installation at that address or
  port, or a rotated key). The issue says roughly this. The tree adds
  that §5's sentence "the host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is
  not its own, so a relayed request … fails" does not hold for a
  browser, and the spec text must say so.
- Cookies are scoped by host, not by port. Two Switchboard instances on
  one Mac (`SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT`, design §3.1) and any other HTTPS
  service on another port of that host would all receive a
  `Secure` cookie set by one of them. A cookie name per `server_id`
  avoids the clash between instances. It does not stop another service
  on that host from receiving it. `localStorage` is per origin
  (scheme, host and port), so it does not have this problem, but any
  script on the origin can read it.

## 4. Rust host

### 4.1 Implementation

- **No Tokio.** The host is std threads and `mpsc`; the core is owned by `SwitchboardApp` and every state change is a dispatch on the frame thread. The remote port follows the `ControlSocket` shape: an accept thread per listener, one thread per connection, each request handed over a channel to the frame, answered by the same `serve` path in `app.rs` (`serve_pending` runs before every frame, hidden ones included), the reply sent back on the connection's channel. A second runtime inside an egui app buys nothing for a handful of connections.
- **The frame does core state only.** A metadata request (a view, a command) is answered on the frame as the control port is. A content request (conversation, screen, run output, file) takes two steps: the frame answers with the **handle and the redaction policy** (the transcript path and resume handle, the pane's host id, the run's log path, the file's root and relative path, plus the secret values to mask and the policy fingerprint), and one **content worker thread** does the read, the parse, the mask, the version check and the serialization from a queue of such requests (one at a time, so one large parse is in memory at once; Spike 22 measured 575 MB peak for the largest transcript), then sends one small action back to the frame to record the version it observed (§4.4), and the connection thread writes the reply. The watch poll (§4.4) runs through the same worker. A multi-megabyte transcript, a 768 KiB file or a slow Keychain call therefore costs the worker its time and the asking connection its wait, never a frame. The handle is read under the frame's authority, so a record removed or rebound between the two steps makes the worker's version action a no-op and the reply carries the handle it read from.
- **Bounds.** The port is one user's few devices, and the limits say so:
  - at most 16 connections in total and 4 unauthenticated ones; a further accept is closed at once. The 4 are a separate pool: an unauthenticated flood fills its own slots and never a paired client's;
  - `/pair` is answered at most six times a minute per listener and `/info` sixty; past that the connection thread answers 429 without reaching the frame;
  - a TLS handshake and the first request line each within 5 s, a request body within 10 s, a write within 10 s; a connection that misses a deadline is closed;
  - one request in flight per connection (HTTP/1.1, no pipelining);
  - the frame drains at most 8 remote requests per pass, in arrival order, the rest waiting on the channel; the channel is bounded at 64 and a full channel answers 503 from the connection thread without reaching the frame; a frame-side request is a view or a handle lookup and takes microseconds, so the count is the bound;
  - each WebSocket subscriber has an event queue of 256; when it fills, the subscriber is sent `resync_required` and closed, never silently trimmed (§4.4);
  - the watch set (§4.4) is capped at 128 keys for the whole port; past the cap the least recently read key is evicted silently, since a read of an evicted key always works and re-enters it.
- Preferred crates: a blocking HTTP/1.1 server over `std::net::TcpListener` (hand-rolled or `tiny_http`), `tungstenite` for WebSocket, `rustls` with `rcgen` for the per-installation certificate, and `mdns-sd` (or the system `dns-sd` through a small macOS adapter) for Bonjour. All of it in `src/adapters/remote.rs` behind a `ports::remote` trait with a fake, and all of it must compile on Linux CI (Bonjour may be a `cfg(target_os = "macos")` adapter with a no-op elsewhere). **Spike 22 (§10) decides the exact crates before any of this is built.**
- Handlers are thin: HTTP request → auth and scope check → allowlist → `wire::Request` → `serve` → redaction → `wire::Reply` → HTTP response. No session or transcript logic lives in the adapter.
- Only the instance holding the store lock listens (as the control port does); a read-only instance refuses to bind.
- Bind to loopback by default until remote access is explicitly enabled in Settings. For LAN access, bind the chosen interface and require pairing.
- Configurable port in `identity.json` (§3.1), default `43187`, overridable with `SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT` (a dev aid, documented in the README) so two instances can run on one machine; `0` picks a free one, which the tests use.
- Advertise `_switchboard._tcp` via Bonjour only while listening on a non-loopback interface. TXT records carry the protocol major version (`v`), the display name (`name`) and the `server_id` (`id`, so a client matches a record to a known server before it connects); never a token, never key material. The instance name is the display name with a short id suffix, so two installations on one machine stay distinct.
- If Switchboard closes, the port goes away. A standalone daemon is not in scope.

### 4.2 API conventions
### 4.3 Endpoints

| Method | Endpoint | Wire body | Scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| GET | `/api/v1/info` | new: `info` | none (identity only, before pairing) |
| POST | `/api/v1/pair` | pairing handshake (§5) | none, only inside the pairing window |
| GET | `/api/v1/projects` | `projects`; `?scope=all` includes Dispatch's worker records | read |
| GET | `/api/v1/spaces` | `spaces` | read |
| GET | `/api/v1/spaces/{id}/sets` | `sets` | read |
| GET | `/api/v1/sets/{id}` | new: `set` (the `SetView` with pins) | read |
| GET | `/api/v1/projects/{id}/sessions` | `sessions`; `?scope=all` as above | read |
| GET | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}` | `session` | read |
| GET | `/api/v1/waiting` | `waiting`; `?scope=all` as above | read |
| GET | `/api/v1/sessions/{id}/screen?lines=n` | `session.screen` | read |
### 4.4 WebSocket events

Envelope:

```json
{
  "server_id": "uuid",
  "epoch": "uuid",
  "revision": 1042,
  "type": "changed",
  "resource": {"kind": "session", "id": "record-uuid"},
  "at_ms": 1760220000000
}
```

Event types:

- `hello {epoch, revision}`: the first frame on every subscription.
- **Scope.** A listing leaves out the records Dispatch made for its own use: a ticket's project with everything in it, and a worker session (the planner, an implementer, a reviewer) in any project, told by the `<ticket>-<nonce>` form of the op they were made under (`switchboard_control::is_dispatch_worker_op`). A supervisor's records (`sup-…`) and the owner's own are listed as ever, and a worker record is still read by its id, which is how the ticket view to come will reach them. `?scope=all` on `projects`, `sessions`, `waiting` and on the `events` subscription lists them and announces them; a plain subscription gets no `project`, `sessions`, `session` or `runs` frame about one. `info` lists `scope` among its capabilities. The point is the wire: hundreds of worker sessions on a host, which the headset fetched one project at a time, are now neither fetched nor announced.
- `changed {kind, id}` with the **metadata kinds** `project`, `space`, `set`, `session`; the **content kinds** `conversation`, `screen`, `run_output` (`id` = `record/n`), `file` (a pinned file, `id` = `project_id/path`); and the collection kinds `projects`, `spaces`, `sets` (with the space's id), `sessions` (with the project's id), `runs` (with the record's id), `waiting`, emitted when a collection's member id set moves and answered by refetching the collection whole; a global collection's `id` is the empty string. Each kind is its own resource key on the client (§4.2); a member fetched as part of its collection holds the collection's revision until it is read alone.
- `removed {kind, id}`: the resource is gone; the client drops it and marks any window on it "removed on <server>".
- `watching {kind, id}`: the answer to a `watch` frame (below).
- `resync_required`: sent before the host closes a subscriber whose queue overflowed; the client reconnects and refetches everything.

**What produces events.** The host has no event bus, and a save is not a reliable sign of a visible change: working sets save through `SaveViews`, Claude Code's trust question (`PromptSeen`) and a Codex pane going quiet (`HostListed`) change what a card says with no save at all. So the port does not watch for saves. Revision and events come from three places in `app.rs`:

1. **The read-model diff, after every pass.** After every `dispatch` and after every polling pass (`HostListed`, the hook log, `Tick`), the app recomputes a cheap per-resource fingerprint of each exported metadata read model (`SessionView`, `SetView` with its members, `ProjectView`, `SpaceView`, `waiting`) and compares it with the previous pass's. One `changed` per resource whose fingerprint moved, one `removed` per resource that vanished, one `changed` per collection whose membership moved, and `revision` bumped once per pass that emitted anything. The diff is the gate, not the effect list, so a set rename, a pin edit, a trust-question transition, a quiet-state transition and a time-based rule-set change all surface without anyone naming them. The fingerprint is a hash over the view's serialized bytes **with its time-derived fields held at zero**: `quiet_secs` is computed from the clock in `session_view` and would move every pass, so the view gains an additive `last_activity_ms` the client derives quiet from, and the quiet **state** (the card's word moving to idle) is what the diff sees. Collections carry the membership revision of §4.2, bumped only when the member id set moves. The hash is cheap at this scale (hundreds of records); the spike measures it (§10).
2. **Content versions, assigned where content is read.** Conversation text, pane text, run output and pinned files are mutable outside the core and can change between two reads inside one poll interval, so a content reply's revision cannot come from the counter alone. Every content read goes through a per-key **content cache** in `SwitchboardApp`, whose bookkeeping lives on the frame and whose reads run on the connection or worker thread (§4.1). The cache holds, per key, the **source version** and the **policy fingerprint of the owning project (§4.3)** it last served, with the revision it was assigned. The source version per kind, chosen so that no change the host can see leaves it unchanged:
   - **transcript**: size and mtime. Claude Code's JSONL only appends, Switchboard never edits one, and `/clear` or a discard rebinds the record to another file, so a growing size is a reliable version and a same-size rewrite does not occur;
   - **pinned file**: inode, ctime and size, read from the descriptor the walk ends on. No user tool preserves ctime, so an editor that rewrites in place, a same-size rewrite, and a replace-by-rename (a new inode) all move it;
   - **run output**: inode, ctime and size of the run's log. A log truncated and regrown to the same length has a new ctime; a rotated one a new inode;
   - **screen**: a hash of the pane text, as today.
   When either the source version or the policy fingerprint differs from what the cache holds, the worker's reply carries the new content and the frame, on the worker's version action, bumps `revision`, emits `changed {content kind, id}`, and stores the new version with that revision; the reply is stamped with that revision. **Two different content versions never share a revision for one key within an epoch**, and two reads of unchanged content return the same bytes and the same revision. The policy is resolved before the read; a resolution failure refuses the reply and leaves the cache untouched, so no earlier masked bytes stand in for the answer. A policy change is also noticed by the diff pass (the `env.*` actions are dispatches), which emits `changed` for every watched content key of the affected project without waiting for a read.
3. **The watch poll.** The port keeps a **watch set**: every content key any subscriber has asked to watch, plus every content key read in the last minute. Independently of the local view, every two seconds a worker thread checks each watched key's source version (a `stat`, or a pane snapshot for `screen`; never a parse) and, for a key that moved, reads it through the content cache, which is what emits the `changed`. The local session view reads its conversation through the same cache (an unmasked variant; §4.3), so the two polls share work rather than duplicate it. The set is capped at 128 keys (§4.1); past that the least recently read key is dropped, and a key with no subscriber and no read for a minute is dropped too. A read of a key not in the set still answers and still versions correctly, since the version is checked on every read; what eviction costs is the `changed` event until the next read, which the client's periodic refetch of a visible view covers.

**Watch frames.** A client sends `watch {kind, id}` when the first view instance on a content key opens and `unwatch` when the last one closes; the client keeps a reference count per key so closing one of two windows on a session changes nothing on the host. The host answers `watching` once the key is in its set, and the client fetches the initial content only after that, so the first snapshot's revision is covered by the poll from then on. A watch is never refused. On reconnect, after `hello`, the client resends every watch with a nonzero count before it snapshots. A visible content view also refetches on its own every thirty seconds, which is what covers a key the host evicted from the set.

**The conversation cache** moves from `UiState` to `SwitchboardApp` as one of the content caches, keyed by record id, resume handle and content version, read by the session view and the port alike; `UiState` keeps a reference, not a copy. This is a frontend change (the session, card and workflow views read the cache), so it is its own commit before any port code, Milestone A0 (§10), with the app behaving identically. This, the diff and the worker handoff are the changes to the app outside the adapter, and §12.6 says why they are required.

**Subscribe first, then snapshot.** A client connecting to a host:

1. opens the WebSocket and waits for `hello {epoch, revision}` (events start flowing at once and are buffered by the client);
2. fetches the snapshots it needs, each reply carrying its own `revision`;
3. applies the buffered events: an event whose `revision` is past a snapshot's `revision` invalidates that resource and is refetched; the rest were already in the snapshot;
4. enables commands.

Because the subscriber is registered on the frame thread before any later pass can bump `revision`, a metadata snapshot is taken on that thread with the revision it carries, and a content reply is stamped on that thread when the worker's version action lands (the same moment its `changed` would be emitted, so the event and the reply name one revision), no change can fall between a subscription and a snapshot. Several snapshots in flight are each reconciled against the buffer by their own revision; events that arrive during a refetch are reconciled the same way, which is why the client never clears its buffer until step 4. A resource named by an event the client has never seen is fetched. If `epoch` differs from the one the client holds (the host restarted), every cached item is stale and is refetched. There is no retained-event replay: a `resync_required` is the only answer to a gap, and events are never durable.

### 4.5 Commands

- `send`, `resume` and `trust` are authenticated actions under `control` scope against one owning server and session.
- The client makes a UUID operation id per command and sends it as the wire `op`.
- **Logged before run.** Today `operations.log` gets a request line only for creations, and the reply line after the command ran; `serve` skips a command only when a reply line exists. That leaves a crash between sending keys and appending the reply as a repeat on retry. The port closes that gap for every non-replayable command (`Class::NonReplayable`: `session.send`, `session.resume`): `serve` appends the request line **before** dispatch, and a failed append refuses the command without running it. On arrival, an op with a request line and no reply line is answered `interrupted` and **not run again**; an op with a reply line is answered from it. `session.trust` is `Idempotent` on the wire and needs neither.
- The client's rule per `/ops/{op}` status:
  - `done`: use the reply;
  - `interrupted`: the host started it and the outcome is unknown; never resubmit; show the session's current state and let the user decide;
  - `unknown`: the host never received it (nothing was logged, and the frame answers queued requests in arrival order, so a request that had reached the frame before the status query has a line); resubmitting with the same op is safe.
  A timeout on a command is followed by a status query, never by a blind resend.
- `send` puts keys into the pane, as the app's own message box does. "Accepted" means the keys were sent. Progress is the record's state: `PromptSubmitted`, then working, then `Stop` with the new last response. A send to a pane sitting at Claude Code's folder trust question is accepted but goes nowhere until `trust` answers it; the session view carries `trust_question`, and the client shows the same "Trust this folder" button the app shows.
- `resume` on a not-running agent is user-initiated, so allowed, but the client confirms it ("Resume spends a turn") before sending; the host never resumes on its own.
- Failures name the reason: not running, not resumable, unknown record, scope missing, pairing revoked, log unavailable.
- **A new session (2026-10-19).** `POST projects/{id}/sessions` under `control` opens a session in the project, through the same `session.new` the CLI and Dispatch use, with the body's `op` as the key: `{op, name, kind, cwd, prompt}`, `kind` one of `claude`, `codex` or `shell` (a command or a service is not opened from a device), `cwd` the project's root when absent and otherwise a directory under it, relative or absolute, refused `bad_request` when it steps out of the root or is not a directory, so a device never opens a shell elsewhere on the disk; `prompt` is an agent's first message, on its command line as the CLI puts it, so the agent is already working when the device opens the window. The reply is the command body with `made: [{kind: "session", id}]`; `/ops/{op}` carries `made` too, so a creation whose reply was lost still names its record. `info` lists `create`. The client offers it on a host that is connected, paired under `control` and serves `create`: a plus button on the Sessions tab and "New session in this project" on a listed session, opening a sheet with the host, the project by workspace, the kind, a name (the kind's word and a count when none is typed), a directory and the first message; Start posts it, reads the project's sessions again and opens the new session's window.

**The draft.** An agent session's prompt on the host is its Prompt Box editor (design.md, "Prompt Box status"), one document with undo, the live utterance as a provisional span, voice commands and the AI pass. A device does not keep a prompt of its own: it reads the editor's draft and works on it, so dictation from the headset, dictation at the desk and typing on either meet in one text, and a prompt begun on one device can be finished on the other. The editor exists whether or not the session is drawn on the host, as it does for a card's microphone.

- `GET sessions/{id}/draft` (any paired device) answers `{draft: {text, live, status, status_text, can_undo, can_redo, ai, busy}}`: the rendered text, the byte range of the utterance still being recognized or null, the editor's status (`idle`, `listening`, `finishing`, `degraded`, `error`) with its reason, whether undo and redo apply, whether the host has an `OpenAI` key for the AI pass, and whether a pass is running. Only an agent session has a draft (`no_draft` otherwise). The host emits `changed {draft, id}` for an editor whose draft moved, fingerprinted a few times a second while a subscriber is connected, and a device holding the draft re-reads it; no watch is needed, since the editor is the host's own state rather than a source the worker polls.
- `POST sessions/{id}/draft` (control) applies one of the editor's tools and answers with the draft as it stands: `{action: "replace", text}` sets the text whole (what the device typed; last writer wins, one person), `undo`, `redo`, `clear`, `clean_up` (the AI pass, refused `failed` when the host has no key), `delete_sentence`, `delete_paragraph`, and `{action: "send", op}`, which takes the draft's text to the pane exactly as `session.send` does, under the device's op as the key, and clears the editor when it went; a repeat of a send that went is answered from the log. A send of an empty draft is refused.
- `POST sessions/{id}/dictation` (control) carries `{session, events}`: the device's recognizer session, a number the device picks apart from the host's own, and its speech events in order, each `{sequence, kind, utterance, revision, text}` with `kind` one of `started`, `voice_started`, `partial`, `final`, `voice_ended`, `stopped`. The host feeds them to the editor as its own recognizer's events: `started` puts the editor's status at listening, a partial is the provisional span revised in place, a final commits the utterance at its anchor, `stopped` returns the status to idle. At most 256 events of 16 KiB each per request. The reply is the draft as it stands, so the device sees its words land without waiting for the event. The device segments speech into utterances itself (the Apple recognizer starts over after a pause and closes an utterance by re-sending its words later); the editor keeps the document. Two recognizers into one editor (the desk's and the headset's) are kept apart by their session numbers.

### 4.6 Dispatch and waiting

"Waiting on you" on a card includes reasons set from outside: Dispatch marks a session through `session.waiting` when one of its tickets needs a decision. `SessionView.waiting_reason` is already on the wire; the client shows it. The `Dispatch · <project>` working sets are ordinary sets to the client.

#### 4.7 Tickets

The ticket view on a device (2026-10-17) reads Dispatch through the Switchboard port, not Dispatch's own socket, which only the Mac reaches: the port serves what the app already holds from its two-second status poll, so a device costs the runner nothing. `GET dispatch/tickets` is the core's `TicketListing` (`src/core/tickets.rs`): `connected` (a runner answered the last poll; without one the tickets are the last seen), the `projects` with a pipeline (slots, running, pending, waiting on me, the queue, the supervisor's session id), and the `tickets` by project then oldest first, never the runner's write order. Each ticket is a summary: source, state and reason, the current stage's name among the `stages`, `standing` worded exactly as the Mac's page words it (`1 waiting on you`, `plan running`, `parked: <reason>`, `held: <why>`), `waits` and `urgent` as the page colours it, `current_session` and `root_project`, and every decision with its question, options, recommendation, `multiple`, state, answer and `needs_note`. `GET dispatch/tickets/{id}` adds the body (bounded at the notes cap), the attempts with the session each ran in and the pull request it is bound to, the lanes by branch, and the holds; paths stay on the Mac. The collection is one resource, `tickets` with an empty id, fingerprinted with everything else: a decision made or answered, a stage moved, or the runner coming or going is one `changed` frame, to every subscriber.

Two commands under `control`, each the Mac's own action and so Dispatch's own call: `decide` takes `{decision, answer, note?}` (the decision's id; for a `multiple` decision the options joined by commas) and is checked against the last status before anything runs (the decision pending, every option among the decision's, a note where the option needs one), and `resume` a parked ticket. The reply is deferred until Dispatch answers the call, through the same channel the content worker answers on: `{decision}` or `{ticket}` on success, the runner's reason as `failed` or `not_found`, `dispatch_off` (503) when no runner answers. A decision already answered as asked is answered again from the record, so a device that lost the reply repeats at no cost; one answered otherwise is `answered` (409). `info` lists `tickets` among the capabilities, and a client treats a host without it as having no tickets.

## 5. Security and pairing

A local network is not a trust boundary: these APIs can instruct coding agents and expose private transcripts. The repo's rules apply unchanged: secret values never reach a record, a log line, a command line, or any reply but `env.resolve` (which is not on this port) and, as redacted text, the read models of §4.3; the Keychain holds key material.

- Require pairing **before** anything but `/info` and `/pair`.
- **Host identity**: a self-signed certificate made once with `rcgen` on first listen. The certificate is in `identity.json` (§3.1); its private key is a Keychain item through the existing adapter (`adapters/keychain.rs`, service `com.sadburger.switchboard`) under the account `remote-key:<server_id>`, so two data directories under one macOS account never overwrite each other's keys. The bundle must be signed with the stable identity (`scripts/bundle.sh`) or the Keychain ACL is lost on every rebuild.
- **What the client pins** is the SPKI SHA-256 of the host's public key, not the certificate's bytes, so a certificate reissued from the same key (a new expiry) still verifies. Rotating the key is making a new identity: every pairing is invalid and the dialog says so.
- **Pairing verifies the key before the code is sent.** The code alone would let an intermediary terminate the first connection, forward the code to the real host, and take the token. So the pairing window shows a **QR code** carrying `{server_id, spki_sha256, code, addresses}`, and under it the same in text: a short form of the key hash and the code. The client scans or types both; it connects, compares the hash of the key it is actually talking to with the one it was given, and only when they match sends `/pair {code, device_name, spki_sha256}`. A client without a camera (visionOS gives an app none) pairs from the host's Bonjour record instead: it resolves the record, reads `/info` under no trust, shows the key the host presented in the dialog's short form for the owner to compare by eye, and pins that key for the pairing, so the typed code reaches only the host whose key the owner che
- The pairing window is opened from the settings menu as "Allow pairing for 5 minutes", the same shape as the environment setup window (`ENV_SETUP_WINDOW`, never saved). The dialog that opens it chooses the scope the pairing grants, `read` by default.
- **The code**: eight characters from the 32-character Crockford alphabet (no `I`, `L`, `O`, `U`), 40 bits, drawn from the OS random source (`getrandom`), made when the window opens and shown as the QR's `code` and in text. It is single-use: the first successful `/pair` consumes it and closes the window. **Failures count globally**: one counter in the app's state, bumped on the frame for every failed `/pair` from any connection, and the window closes at three. Concurrent attempts cannot each get three, because the frame answers them in arrival order against the one counter.
- **The token**: 32 bytes from the OS random source, base64url, 43 characters. It does not expire; the owner revokes. It is sent only as a bearer header over the pinned connection, never in a URL.
- `/pair` answers with the token and the granted scope. The host stores the device name, scope, created time, last-seen time and the token's SHA-256 in `<data dir>/devices.json` (atomic write, owner-readable); never the token. The client stores the token and the pinned key hash in its Keychain.
- **Scope changes** happen in the host's dialog: a device's scope can be raised to `control` or lowered to `read` there, taking effect on the device's next request. There is no scope request over the port.
- **Key rotation** (a missing key at listen, §3.1) **deletes every record in `devices.json`** when the new identity is made, so an old token stops working on the first request, and the dialog says the pairings are gone. A client seeing a new key for a known `server_id` shows "identity changed, pair again" and sends nothing, token included.
- Every later request carries the bearer token; the host answers with the device's scope. A Settings dialog (built the way the Environment dialog is) lists paired devices with scope, last seen, and Revoke, and states what redaction does and does not cover. Revocation removes the record, takes effect on the next request and closes the device's WebSocket.
- The client verifies the pin on every connection and on endpoint changes; a mismatch is shown as "identity changed, pair again" and never auto-merged.
- Validate input, cap request bodies at 64 KiB, cap `lines` on `screen` (the wire clamps to 200) and `run_output` (500), cap pages and bodies as §4.2 says, and keep tokens out of logs, URLs, Bonjour TXT records and crash reports. Refusals are logged by op and kind, never with content.
- Loopback-only without auth is acceptable **only inside the spike directory**. No milestone commit binds a non-loopback interface without pairing.

## 9. Remote access later

Every server is an authenticated endpoint; nothing assumes RFC1918 addresses or Bonjour. A future Tailscale or WireGuard route, a manual remote endpoint, or an outbound relay reuses the same protocol, token and pinned key. No relay in v1. The pin is bound to the installation's key, not to an address or a certificate's validity window, so a route change or a reissued certificate does not invalidate it.

# Plan: a web control surface on the remote port (#230)

Line numbers are as they are in this worktree at 7fe8949. The facts file
is cited as `facts.md` with its section; "Settled" lines are used as
written, "Unresolved" and "For the owner" lines are named where a decision
rests on one.

The default everywhere below is the design that works whichever way the
open questions are answered: the page pairs and reads over `fetch` with a
bearer header, and treats the events socket as an upgrade it may lose. The
cookie transport and the socket are built, and switch on by a constant
once the owner has run the page on a phone.

## Where this departs from the issue

- **"The one-line excerpt the card shows" does not exist.** The notes and
  `facts.md` (Settled, The tree) say `last_message` is on the session
  record. It is not. It is a field of the hook event
  `EventKind::Stopped { last_message, .. }` (`src/ports/events.rs:24`) and
  the core drops it: `src/core/events.rs:132` matches
  `Stopped { pending, .. }`. `SessionRecord` has no such field and
  `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:637-688`) has none either. So the
  list shows what the wire has: kind, `card` (the card's word), `waiting`
  and `waiting_reason`. The last response appears only in the session view.
  No new read model, no `SessionView` field, no fixture change.
- **"The device's scope in the header" has no source after pairing.** No
  endpoint returns it (`remote_info`, `src/app.rs:3568`, is unauthenticated).
  The page keeps the scope from the `/pair` reply and corrects it when a
  `send` is refused with code `scope` (`src/app.rs:3166-3171`).
- **"Revoked" cannot be told from "never paired" by the code.** Both
  refusals in `authenticate` (`src/app.rs:3127-3152`) are `unauthorized`.
  The page keeps a non-secret marker (server id, key hash, device id, name,
  scope). A 401 with a marker says "this device is no longer paired"; a
  401 without one says "open the pairing window on the host". The host
  adds no code.
- **"Any path outside `/api/v1/` is refused" is true, but late.**
  `serve_remote` does it (`src/app.rs:3023`) after the request took a slot
  in the frame's inbox of 64. The static paths and the 404 for every other
  non-API path are now answered on the connection thread.
- **§5's relay sentence does not hold for a browser.**
  `docs/remote-client.md` §5 says the host's own key check in `/pair` makes
  a relayed request fail. `remote_pair` (`src/app.rs:3636`) compares the
  key in the request body, and under a relay the body comes from the
  impostor's page. The page's `key` check catches a genuine page talking to
  the wrong genuine host (another installation at that address, a rotated
  key). It cannot see the certificate it is on. The spec text is amended
  to say so.
- **`facts.md` says `RemoteReply` is built at about 15 sites.** The tree
  has 11 struct literals: ten in `src/app.rs` (`:1664`, `:1679`, `:2365`,
  `:2371`, `:2376`, `:2754`, `:3570`, `:3723`, `:3736`, `:3767`) and one in
  `src/adapters/remote.rs:829`. No file under `tests/` builds one.
- **An existing test changes.** `tests/ui.rs:7474-7490` parses the copied
  invite as JSON; it becomes a URL.

Decisions the issue asks the plan to settle:

1. **Trust: the click-through is the trust step, said in the dialog; the
   certificate is not offered for download.** A download only helps if the
   device then trusts a manually installed certificate, which needs the
   certificate to meet Apple's rules (`facts.md`, Settled, Apple's TLS
   rules; the tree confirms the current one meets none of SAN, `serverAuth`
   or 825 days: `make_identity`, `src/adapters/remote.rs:102-110`). Whether
   Safari lets the owner proceed at all, and whether the exception then
   covers `fetch` and `wss`, is Unresolved 1 and 2 and For the owner A; the
   plan does not wait on them. It reissues the certificate over the same
   key with the IP and the `.local` name as SANs, `serverAuth` and a
   validity of at most 825 days (Unresolved 1, 2, 3: helps in every
   branch, costs nothing if unneeded). A profile or a download is a later
   issue if A says the click-through is not enough. §5's rule becomes: no
   non-loopback bind serves anything but `/info`, `/pair` and the page's
   three files before pairing; the files are the same bytes for everyone
   and carry no secret.
2. **Token transport: the bearer header on `fetch`, a subprotocol value on
   the socket, the cookie built behind them.** The default needs no browser
   behaviour that `facts.md` leaves open: headers on `fetch` work
   everywhere, and a base64url token is a legal subprotocol token (Settled,
   RFC 6455). The cookie needs Unresolved 5 and For the owner D to be
   favourable, so it is the enhancement (`TRANSPORT` in `app.js`, `'token'`
   by default). The token sits in `localStorage` under the default,
   readable only by this origin's scripts: the CSP (no inline script, no
   external one) leaves the page's own script as the only reader. Under the
   cookie it is not stored at all.
3. **One QR, the URL.** Nothing generates the JSON any more. The Swift
   parser keeps decoding JSON (the visionOS paste field and old pasted
   text), so no client breaks.
4. **Static paths** are in The signals below.
5. **Where the page lives and how it is tested:** `web/`, embedded; the
   tests are in The tests.
6. **The device record: the name only.** The page sends `device_name` from
   its user agent ("Safari on iPhone"); `new_device` already cuts it to 64
   characters (`src/core/remote.rs`, `new_device`). No `kind` field.

## The record

- **`identity.json` gains two additive fields**, `certificate_names:
  Vec<String>` and `certificate_expires: Option<SystemTime>`, both
  `#[serde(default)]`, so the host knows what the stored certificate
  covers without parsing it. `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION`
  (`src/ports/remote.rs:17`) is bumped: **the value in that file at
  implementation time, plus one** (it is 1 today; a ticket landing in
  parallel may take the next number first). An older file reads with empty
  names, which means "reissue at the next bind". `RemoteFiles::load_identity`
  (`src/adapters/remote.rs:74`) already refuses a newer file. `model.rs`
  and its `SCHEMA_VERSION` (16 today) are untouched; `devices.json` is
  unversioned and unchanged.
- **Rehydration.** The key stays in the Keychain under
  `Identity::key_account`. `bind_remote` (`src/app.rs:2936`) already reads
  the key and builds the TLS config; it now first compares the identity's
  names and expiry with what this machine answers to (the outward IP from
  `local_address()`, `127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, and `<LocalHostName>.local`)
  and a 30-day margin. On a miss it reissues over the same key with
  `rcgen::KeyPair::from_pem` (as `spki_sha256_of_key` does,
  `src/adapters/remote.rs:138-141`), so `spki_sha256` and every pairing are
  unchanged (`facts.md`, Settled: the certificate can be reissued over the
  same key). It saves `identity.json` through the existing atomic path
  directly, as `make_identity` in `app.rs` does at load, then dispatches
  `AppAction::CertificateReissued`. It does not go through
  `Effect::SaveIdentity`: that arm rebinds when `remote_bound` differs
  (`src/app.rs:2895-2898`), and `bind_remote` has just cleared it.
- An address that moves after the bind is not covered until the next
  bind. The pairing dialog says so when `local_address()` is not in
  `certificate_names` and names the fix (turn "Local network" off and on,
  which rebinds); the page's warning interstitial is then the one the owner
  already knows (Unresolved 7: an address change is another warning).
- The page keeps one non-secret marker in `localStorage`: server id, key
  hash, device id, name, scope, host name. The token is a second entry
  under the default transport.

## The signals

No new event. The page speaks the existing protocol: `GET info`, `POST
pair`, `GET waiting`, `GET projects`, `GET projects/{id}/sessions`, `GET
sessions/{id}/last-response` (`screen` for a non-Claude kind), `POST
sessions/{id}/send`, `GET ops/{op}`, and the `events` socket with `watch`
frames for the content key (`conversation` for `last-response`, `screen`).

- **Reads and revisions.** Subscribe first, then snapshot (§4.4). Each
  reply carries `epoch` and `revision`; a reply older than what the page
  holds for that resource is dropped, a new `epoch` refetches everything,
  `resync_required` reconnects and refetches.
- **Polling is the floor, the socket the upgrade** (`facts.md`
  Unresolved 1; the plan never waits on it). The list and the open
  session are refetched every 3 s when no socket is connected and every 30
  s when one is (§4.4's visible-view refetch). A socket that fails to
  open, or closes, shows "live updates unavailable" and the page carries
  on polling; it retries the socket every 30 s. Acceptance step 4 (a
  session moves to the top without a reload) therefore holds on either
  branch, within 3 s without the socket and at once with it.
- **Operation ids.** `crypto.randomUUID()` only when
  `window.isSecureContext`, else 16 bytes of `getRandomValues` as hex
  (Unresolved 4). A `send` that times out is checked with `GET ops/{op}`,
  never resent (§4.5).
- **The pairing URL.**
  `https://<ip>:<port>/?code=<code>&key=<spki_sha256>&id=<server_id>`, an
  IPv6 host in brackets. The host part is the outward IP from
  `local_address()`; the `.local` name goes in only if the owner answers
  For the owner B favourably, a one-line change in the dialog, since the
  certificate already covers both (Unresolved 9). On load the page, before
  any request: reads the query, calls `history.replaceState(null, '',
  location.pathname)`, then `GET /api/v1/info`, then compares `key` with
  `spki_sha256` and `id` with `server_id`, and posts `/pair` only on a
  match. On a mismatch it says "this is not the host whose code was
  scanned" and sends nothing. With a marker whose server id matches but
  whose key differs from `/info`'s, it says "identity changed, pair again"
  and sends nothing, token included (§5).
- **The code in history.** Unresolved 6 and For the owner C: whether the

  charset=utf-8`). Each answers with `Cache-Control: no-store`,

  default transports are not ambient. The host still checks `Origin`

# Plan: a web control surface on the remote port (#230)

Line numbers are as they are in this worktree at 7fe8949. The facts file
is cited as `facts.md` with its section; "Settled" lines are used as
written, "Unresolved" and "For the owner" lines are named where a decision
rests on one.

The default everywhere below is the design that works whichever way the
open questions are answered: the page pairs and reads over `fetch` with a
bearer header, and treats the events socket as an upgrade it may lose. The
cookie transport and the socket are built, and switch on by a constant
once the owner has run the page on a phone.

## Where this departs from the issue

- **"The one-line excerpt the card shows" does not exist.** The notes and
  `facts.md` (Settled, The tree) say `last_message` is on the session
  record. It is not. It is a field of the hook event
  `EventKind::Stopped { last_message, .. }` (`src/ports/events.rs:24`) and
  the core drops it: `src/core/events.rs:132` matches
  `Stopped { pending, .. }`. `SessionRecord` has no such field and
  `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:637-688`) has none either. So the
  list shows what the wire has: kind, `card` (the card's word), `waiting`
  and `waiting_reason`. The last response appears only in the session view.
  No new read model, no `SessionView` field, no fixture change.
- **"The device's scope in the header" has no source after pairing.** No
  endpoint returns it (`remote_info`, `src/app.rs:3568`, is unauthenticated).
  The page keeps the scope from the `/pair` reply and corrects it when a
  `send` is refused with code `scope` (`src/app.rs:3166-3171`).
- **"Revoked" cannot be told from "never paired" by the code.** Both
  refusals in `authenticate` (`src/app.rs:3127-3152`) are `unauthorized`.
  The page keeps a non-secret marker (server id, key hash, device id, name,
  scope). A 401 with a marker says "this device is no longer paired"; a
  401 without one says "open the pairing window on the host". The host
  adds no code.
- **"Any path outside `/api/v1/` is refused" is true, but late.**
  `serve_remote` does it (`src/app.rs:3023`) after the request took a slot
  in the frame's inbox of 64. The static paths and the 404 for every other
  non-API path are now answered on the connection thread.
- **§5's relay sentence does not hold for a browser.**
  `docs/remote-client.md` §5 says the host's own key check in `/pair` makes
  a relayed request fail. `remote_pair` (`src/app.rs:3636`) compares the
  key in the request body, and under a relay the body comes from the
  impostor's page. The page's `key` check catches a genuine page talking to
  the wrong genuine host (another installation at that address, a rotated
  key). It cannot see the certificate it is on. The spec text is amended
  to say so.
- **`facts.md` says `RemoteReply` is built at about 15 sites.** The tree
  has 11 struct literals: ten in `src/app.rs` (`:1664`, `:1679`, `:2365`,
  `:2371`, `:2376`, `:2754`, `:3570`, `:3723`, `:3736`, `:3767`) and one in

- **An existing test changes.** `tests/ui.rs:7474-7490` parses the copied
  invite as JSON; it becomes a URL.

1. **Trust: the click-through is the trust step, said in the dialog; the

   device then trusts a manually installed certificate, which needs the

   external one) leaves the page's own script as the only reader. Under the

4. **Static paths** are in The signals below.

Line numbers are as they are in this worktree at 7fe8949. The facts file
is cited as `facts.md` with its section; "Settled" lines are used as
written, "Unresolved" and "For the owner" lines are named where a decision
rests on one.

The default everywhere below is the design that works whichever way the
open questions are answered: the page pairs and reads over `fetch` with a
bearer header, and treats the events socket as an upgrade it may lose. The
cookie transport and the socket are built, and switch on by a constant
once the owner has run the page on a phone.

## Where this departs from the issue

- **"The one-line excerpt the card shows" does not exist.** The notes and
  `facts.md` (Settled, The tree) say `last_message` is on the session
  record. It is not. It is a field of the hook event
  `EventKind::Stopped { last_message, .. }` (`src/ports/events.rs:24`) and
  the core drops it: `src/core/events.rs:132` matches
  `Stopped { pending, .. }`. `SessionRecord` has no such field and
  `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:637-688`) has none either. So the
  list shows what the wire has: kind, `card` (the card's word), `waiting`
  and `waiting_reason`. The last response appears only in the session view.
  No new read model, no `SessionView` field, no fixture change.
- **"The device's scope in the header" has no source after pairing.** No
  endpoint returns it (`remote_info`, `src/app.rs:3568`, is unauthenticated).
  The page keeps the scope from the `/pair` reply and corrects it when a
  `send` is refused with code `scope` (`src/app.rs:3166-3171`).
- **"Revoked" cannot be told from "never paired" by the code.** Both
  refusals in `authenticate` (`src/app.rs:3127-3152`) are `unauthorized`.
  The page keeps a non-secret marker (server id, key hash, device id, name,
  scope). A 401 with a marker says "this device is no longer paired"; a
  401 without one says "open the pairing window on the host". The host
  adds no code.
- **"Any path outside `/api/v1/` is refused" is true, but late.**
  `serve_remote` does it (`src/app.rs:3023`) after the request took a slot
  in the frame's inbox of 64. The static paths and the 404 for every other
  non-API path are now answered on the connection thread.
- **§5's relay sentence does not hold for a browser.**
  `docs/remote-client.md` §5 says the host's own key check in `/pair` makes
  a relayed request fail. `remote_pair` (`src/app.rs:3636`) compares the
  key in the request body, and under a relay the body comes from the
  impostor's page. The page's `key` check catches a genuine page talking to
  the wrong genuine host (another installation at that address, a rotated
  key). It cannot see the certificate it is on. The spec text is amended
  to say so.
- **`facts.md` says `RemoteReply` is built at about 15 sites.** The tree
  has 11 struct literals: ten in `src/app.rs` (`:1664`, `:1679`, `:2365`,
